opus-5.5.text:
I think a big part of it is that physical tasks have been under evolutionary optimization pressure for a very long time, while abstract theoretical work hasn't. Things like walking, running, grasping objects, and coordinating your body have mattered for survival for hundreds of millions of years. So evolution has pushed most people fairly close to some ceiling on those capabilities. There's still variation, the fastest sprinter is faster than the average person, but if you compare them in relative terms the gap isn't enormous. Usain Bolt is maybe twice as fast as an ordinary person over a hundred meters, not a hundred times faster.

With something like mathematics, theoretical physics, or advanced software engineering, the picture is very different. Those activities are extremely recent on evolutionary timescales. Our brains weren't built for them; we're repurposing general cognitive machinery that evolved for other things. Because there was never strong selection specifically for being good at, say, proving theorems, there's no reason to expect the population to be clustered near any optimum. So small differences in underlying cognitive traits, like working memory, how fast you learn, or how well you hold abstract structure in your head, can compound into huge differences in output. One exceptional researcher might produce more valuable work than dozens or hundreds of average practitioners.

There's also a compounding effect in how these skills are acquired. In technical domains, learning builds on itself. If you're somewhat better at absorbing new ideas, you get further faster, which lets you absorb even more advanced ideas, and the advantage snowballs over a career. Physical performance tends to saturate much more quickly because you hit hard biological limits: muscle physiology, joint mechanics, metabolism.

I think this matters for thinking about AI too. If human performance on cognitive tasks is spread out this widely, it suggests we're nowhere near the ceiling of what's possible. The gap between an average person and a top researcher hints at how much further capabilities could go, and AI systems might not be constrained by the same limits that keep even the best humans where they are. It also means that once AI reaches roughly human level in some domain, it may move through the human range quite quickly in some respects, though I'd be cautious, because the relevant bottlenecks for AI aren't necessarily the same as for people.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts modest relative gaps in physical performance with huge differences in technical output, including one researcher producing more than dozens or hundreds of average practitioners.

r002.rationale: It says theoretical and technical activities are recent on evolutionary timescales, that brains were not built for them, and that humans repurpose general cognitive machinery for these tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing is that the range of outcomes you can actually observe is much wider on the theoretical and technical side, and that's mostly a fact about the tasks, not about people. If you look at something like running, the fastest human in the world runs maybe twice as fast as an ordinary healthy adult. There's a hard physical ceiling, the gap between an elite sprinter and a decent amateur is a few tenths of a second over a hundred meters, and most of the population is compressed into a fairly narrow band. The same holds for lifting, throwing, manual dexterity. You get variation, but it's bounded, and the bounds are set by physics and physiology.

With intellectual work, especially research, there's no comparable ceiling. The output isn't "how fast can you do this fixed thing," it's "can you do this at all," and a lot of the value is concentrated in problems where most people would get nowhere no matter how long they tried. So the distribution of outcomes becomes extremely heavy-tailed. One mathematician might prove a theorem that a thousand others wouldn't have proved in their lifetimes, and there's no physical analogue to that. Nobody runs a marathon a thousand times faster than anyone else.

Part of this is also that cognitive tasks are compositional in a way physical ones mostly aren't. If you're a bit better at each of ten sub-skills, those advantages multiply rather than add, so small differences in underlying ability get amplified into enormous differences in what you can ultimately accomplish. And then on top of that you have accumulation. Knowledge builds on itself. Someone who understands a field a little better learns the next thing faster, which widens the gap further over a career. Physical skill accumulates too, but it saturates quickly and then declines with age.

I'd also say some of the apparent difference is measurement. We measure physical ability on scales designed to be comparable, like time and weight, so the compression is visible. For intellectual work we often don't have good units, and we tend to notice only the tail, the people who did something remarkable. If you measured, say, speed of doing routine arithmetic, you'd probably find something that looks more like the physical case, with a modest spread. It's specifically the open-ended, unbounded tasks where the variation explodes.

So my short answer is that physical tasks have ceilings and intellectual tasks largely don't, and when you remove the ceiling, the multiplicative structure of skill and the compounding of knowledge over time produce the heavy tails we see.

r001.rationale: The response says outcomes vary far more on theoretical and technical work, describing intellectual work as extremely heavy-tailed compared with bounded physical performance.

r002.rationale: It explains the variation through task ceilings, multiplicative skills, and accumulating knowledge, but does not attribute it to humans not having evolved for those tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of the difference is in how ability translates into performance. If you’re comparing how fast people can run, the variation is relatively small. An exceptional runner might be twice as fast as an ordinary person, but they’re not a hundred times as fast. Whereas in mathematics or programming, one person might solve a problem in an afternoon that another person couldn’t solve even if you gave them years.

But that doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying variation in cognitive ability is vastly larger. A task can have a threshold: you need to be able to hold enough pieces of the problem in your head, or find the right abstraction, before you can make progress. Relatively modest differences in the abilities that support that can produce very large differences in the outcome.

And knowledge compounds. Understanding one thing makes it easier to learn the next thing, so differences in background, interest, and practice can accumulate. What we observe as technical performance is the result of all of those factors interacting.

It also matters what you measure. If you measured physical ability by whether someone could clear a particular height in the high jump, you’d see a sharp divide between people who could do it and people who couldn’t. So part of the contrast is that we often measure physical performance on a continuous scale, while theoretical work gets measured by whether you solved the problem at all.

r001.rationale: It contrasts the relatively small variation in running speed with cases where one person solves a math or programming problem in an afternoon while another could not solve it in years.

r002.rationale: It explains performance gaps through thresholds, accumulated knowledge, and measurement choices, but does not attribute them to humans not having evolved for those tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of the explanation is that theoretical and technical tasks let small differences in ability compound much more. If you’re running a hundred meters, you’re doing roughly the same thing as everyone else, and there’s a fairly narrow range of speeds that a human body can achieve. Someone who’s twice as fast as an average person is already extraordinary.

But with a mathematical problem, a slightly better understanding might let you notice a shortcut that someone else never finds. You might solve it in ten minutes while they spend a week on it, or never solve it at all. So a modest difference in some underlying ability can translate into an enormous difference in performance.

There’s also a measurement issue. If you measured physical performance by whether someone could clear a particular height, you’d see a sharp divide between people who can and people who can’t. A lot of intellectual tasks are measured in that way: did you find the proof, did you get the program to work? That can make differences look much larger than they would on a smoother measure of ability.

r001.rationale: It explains that modest ability differences can produce enormous performance gaps on mathematical problems, while physical performance has a narrower range.

r002.rationale: It attributes the gap to compounding ability differences and measurement effects, but does not say humans have not evolved to perform theoretical or technical tasks.
